checkpoints: A free-form string log line can only be searched by substring grep and cannot be filtered by user or aggregated by order, because to a machine the whole line is just an opaque string of characters.

A structured JSON line shaped like { msg, orderId, userId, reqId, level } is indexed BY FIELD by the log platform, letting it filter exactly by reqId, aggregate by userId, or alert precisely on level with no regex guessing.

The cost of structure is human readability when eyeballing a raw terminal; that cost is solved by pretty-printing logs locally while still shipping raw JSON in production — because in production the consumer of the log is the log platform, not a human's eyes.
Structure is the precondition for the correlation story: only because every log line is a JSON object can the logger automatically inject a request-scoped ID as a field on every single line.
That automatic per-line ID injection is exactly what makes "give me exactly this request's lines" possible during an incident.
The specific logger library differs per stack (Pino, Logback JSON encoder, Serilog, slog-zap), but the outcome — one JSON object per line — is identical across all of them.

Liveness answers "should I restart this pod?" — the action is kill-and-restart, which is destructive and fleet-wide amplifying if every replica fails it at once, so liveness must check ONLY conditions a restart can actually repair (a deadlock, a wedged in-process pool, something a fresh process fixes just by existing).

Readiness answers a different question — "should I send traffic to this pod?" — and its action is gentle and self-correcting: the pod is pulled from the Service load balancer's rotation with no restart, and added back automatically once the check passes again.

Because readiness's remedy can never make things worse, readiness is free to check the entire dependency graph the pod actually needs to serve a correct response, including the database, cache, and anything else.

Startup answers a third question — "has this pod finished warming up?" — and while it is still failing, the kubelet suspends both liveness and readiness, so a lengthy migration or cold cache fill during boot isn't misread as a crash and killed before the app ever serves a request.

A catch-all /health endpoint checking every dependency, wired to the liveness probe, fails because a downstream outage unrelated to the process itself (like the cache going down) fails every replica's liveness check simultaneously.
Kubernetes then responds to that simultaneous failure by restart-looping the whole deployment, even though restarting the application can never bring the cache back.
The three probes exist precisely so each question gets matched to the action that is actually appropriate for it.

Sentry's Nest integration captures the request body and headers on any event tied to a handler, so without a beforeSend hook, an endpoint like /auth/login that accepts email and password in the body will ship that raw data to Sentry's servers the moment it throws.

beforeSend is the single hook that runs on every event right before delivery, making it the only reliable place to strip or mask sensitive fields such as password, email, authorization headers, and cookies before they leave the process.

Allow-listing the fields that are safe to keep in captured events is more robust than deny-listing sensitive keys by name, because breadcrumbs and nested payload fields commonly escape a deny-list's default scrubbing.

Setting tracePropagationTargets to a catch-all regex like /.*/ causes the SDK to attach sentry-trace and baggage headers — carrying metadata such as release and environment — to every outgoing request the backend makes, including calls to third-party services that never asked to participate in the trace.

Scoping tracePropagationTargets to the API's own real origins (e.g., the frontend's domain and localhost in dev) preserves frontend-to-backend trace stitching while stopping trace metadata from leaking to unrelated third-party hosts.

A tracesSampleRate of 1.0 in production traces every transaction, which burns event quota and adds latency-tracking overhead on every request regardless of whether anyone inspects it; dropping it an order of magnitude (e.g., 0.1) while keeping replaysOnErrorSampleRate at 1.0 preserves full session-replay detail for actual errors while cutting the cost of routine traffic.

An undisclosed PII leak carries more risk than a metadata leak, which in turn carries more risk than a sampling-cost issue, so ranking findings by blast radius — compliance exposure first, third-party data exposure second, cost/overhead third — matters more than the order they appear in the code.

Confirming a fix works requires triggering a captured error through the affected endpoint with a real payload and checking that the delivered event shows masked placeholders instead of raw values, watching for outbound requests to external domains without trace headers attached, and comparing transaction volume in the quota dashboard before and after a sample-rate change.

A half-open TCP connection — where the far end vanished without sending a FIN or RST — gives the socket no signal that anything is wrong, so a raw `await` on a ping call has nothing to resolve or reject against and can hang indefinitely.

Leaving that await unbounded means the only thing that eventually ends the request is the platform's own probe timeout, so a single hung dependency call turns into a stalled readiness probe with concurrent requests piling up behind it in the meantime.

Racing the dependency call against a hard timer, e.g. `Promise.race([client.ping(), timeoutPromise])`, bounds the check itself so whichever settles first wins — a hung dependency becomes a deterministic fast rejection instead of an indefinite stall.
The internal timeout budget must be strictly shorter than the platform probe's own `timeoutSeconds`, so the application decides and reports the failure before the platform gives up on its own.

Setting `maxRetriesPerRequest` to a small bounded value such as 1 makes a broken connection surface an error after one attempt instead of retrying forever, which is what happens when it is left unbounded (`null`).
Disabling the offline command queue (`enableOfflineQueue: false`) makes commands issued while disconnected reject immediately instead of silently queueing and buffering behind the outage.

A cleanly-down dependency and a hung half-open one are different failure mechanisms but must map to the same unhealthy response, since from the platform's point of view the pod cannot serve traffic that needs the dependency either way.

Pausing the dependency's container rather than stopping it freezes the process while leaving the socket open with no reset, reproducing the half-open hang for verification — a clean stop instead resets the TCP connection immediately and only exercises the easy failure path.

A tracing backend such as Jaeger indexes spans by attribute key to support filtering and search, so a key whose value is different on every single request produces a brand-new index entry each time — that unbounded-cardinality growth, not the volume of exported spans, is what balloons storage and cost under production traffic.

The OTLP/Jaeger export path is not the culprit: a BatchSpanProcessor collects finished spans and ships them out-of-band and asynchronously, so it adds negligible per-request latency and does not explain a storage bill that keeps growing with traffic.

Calling `span.setAttribute("http.full_url", req.originalUrl)` bakes the concrete request path — including a fresh order id on every call — into the attribute value, so this single line generates an unbounded set of distinct values for that key across requests.

Calling `span.setAttribute("promo.note", req.body.note)` echoes raw, freeform user-supplied text directly into a span attribute, which is an even less bounded cardinality source than the URL and also risks leaking arbitrary user input into observability data.

The fix for the URL attribute is to replace it with the route template (e.g. `req.route?.path`, a fixed string like `/api/v1/orders/:id/charge`) rather than the concrete path, and to store the order id separately in its own explicitly named attribute such as `order.id` so it stays available for per-order tracing without polluting an unbounded key.
Freeform fields like `promo.note` should be dropped from spans entirely, or hashed/truncated before being attached, since raw user input should never be echoed verbatim into an attribute value.

Reducing attribute cardinality and reducing trace volume are two separate, complementary levers: normalizing attributes controls how much data each stored span carries, while sampling — for example a `ParentBasedSampler` wrapping `TraceIdRatioBasedSampler` in the SDK, or tail sampling at the OpenTelemetry Collector — controls how many spans get stored in the first place.

A sampling strategy for production traffic must still guarantee that traces containing an error (spans with `recordException` or an `ERROR` status) are always kept, so failure visibility is preserved even while the overall sampled fraction is reduced.

After trimming attributes and adding sampling, the change should be verified by comparing span volume and storage growth before and after, and by re-running a real latency investigation to confirm the parent span still leads down into the child span (e.g. `orders.charge`) needed to pinpoint which hop is slow.
The contract has three endpoints — live, ready, startup — with one load-bearing rule: the third-party payment API must never gate any probe.

Liveness checks only the DB connection pool, since a broken pool is repaired by a fresh process; the cache and especially the payment API are excluded because restarting the pod fixes neither, and wiring the payment API into liveness would make the whole fleet fail liveness together the moment that provider blips, causing Kubernetes to restart-loop the deployment over something a restart can never repair.

Readiness checks DB + cache — exactly the dependency set needed to serve a normal response — because readiness's failure mode is gentle: it only pulls the pod from the load balancer and re-adds it automatically once the check passes.

The payment API is excluded from readiness too, since it only touches checkout: wiring it in would let a single slow payment provider yank the entire pod out of traffic, blocking unrelated requests like browsing or search; the correct place to protect against that is a timeout plus circuit breaker at the payment call site itself, not the probe mechanism.

Every check in live/ready races a hard timeout of roughly 2 seconds, which must be shorter than the platform probe's own timeoutSeconds, otherwise the kubelet decides on its own timeout before the app ever returns a verdict.

Because the service boots slowly due to migrations, it needs a startup probe with a generous failure budget: while it still fails, liveness/readiness are suspended so the migration isn't mistaken for a crash and the pod isn't killed before it can serve.

failureThreshold/successThreshold create two-way hysteresis (N consecutive failures before the pod is declared unready, M consecutive passes before it's trusted as ready again), which combined with tight per-check timeouts distinguishes a momentary spike from a real outage and prevents the pod from flapping and amplifying that spike.

Governing principle: every placement decision is defended by the exact action it triggers at the platform level (restart is destructive, readiness's traffic-gate is gentle, startup's grace is suspensive) — a dependency only earns a place in a probe if that action actually fixes its failure.

The contract has four mandatory clauses — an ingress trust boundary, implicit in-process context, mandatory echo at egress, and a rule for work detaching from the async chain — and dropping any one breaks the trace chain exactly where it matters most.
At ingress, a single middleware decides the ID exactly once per request: honor x-request-id if the client sent one (since that's what lets one ID span multiple services), otherwise mint a fresh UUID.

Because that header is fully client-controlled and a potential attack vector, the contract must cap its maximum length, restrict its charset to prevent log injection, and — in zero-trust environments — only honor it when it arrives from a verified trusted upstream proxy, minting a fresh ID for any other source.

In-process, the ID travels through an implicit request-scoped context (AsyncLocalStorage, MDC, LogContext, or context.Context depending on the stack) that lets any nested code read the current ID without it being passed in.

Threading the ID through function arguments and stashing it on the request object both fail structurally — the former pollutes every signature across the call chain and still misses third-party library logs, the latter only helps code that already holds the request — and the store is isolated per request so concurrent requests never mix up IDs.

At egress, the ID must be set on the response header before the handler runs (not only after a successful return) so that even an error response like 404/500 carries the same ID, and it must be forwarded unchanged on any downstream call so the trace chain doesn't break into disconnected segments per hop.

For work that detaches from the request's async chain (a bare timer, a callback from an external event, a job pushed onto a queue), the store is lost because it's bound to the original request's logical chain rather than real time, so the contract mandates capturing the ID into a plain variable before detaching and passing it explicitly into the detached task.

Compliance must be verifiable, not just promised: an echo test (ID in, response returns the exact same ID), a cross-hop test (logs at every service share one ID), a failing-path test (response header still carries the ID even when the handler throws), and a test rejecting an oversized or hostile-charset header.
The correlation ID is decided once, up front, by ingress middleware on order-service before anything else runs.
If the caller already sent an x-request-id (browser retry, partner API, upstream service), that value is honored so the whole chain shares one id; if none arrives, order-service mints a fresh one.

That same middleware writes the id onto the response header before calling the handler, so even when payment-service's debit call throws and the chain returns a 500, the customer's failing response still carries the id — support can read it straight off the error, no timestamps or guesswork needed.

Inside each service, the id lives in an implicit request-scoped context (AsyncLocalStorage on Node, MDC on Java, LogContext on .NET, context.Context on Go), and the structured JSON logger reads whatever is current in that store on every line it writes — including a line buried deep inside payment-service that never received the id as an argument.
Because each request gets its own isolated store, concurrent checkouts running at the same time never cross-contaminate each other's log lines.

Triage is a field filter: pull the x-request-id from the customer's failing response (or find the first matching line by time+endpoint if unavailable), then query the log platform for reqId=<that value> across all three services to get every line belonging to that one request, in order.
The frontend's global error boundary captures the blank-screen exception with a session replay attached, so the user's last clicks can be watched exactly as they happened.
The captured event carries a release equal to the build's commit SHA, and source maps uploaded in CI for that same SHA de-minify the stack trace back to a real file and line.

The page's API call carried the sentry-trace and baggage headers; the backend read them and continued that same trace instead of opening a new one, so the frontend error and the backend's 500 transaction share one trace ID linking the broken page directly to the exact failing request handler.

This is findable in seconds because the capture policy is quiet by default — 201s and valid 4xx never reach the tracker — so the 500 spike stands out as real signal instead of being lost among normal traffic.
The stitching mechanism itself is just two HTTP headers, so it works identically regardless of which language the backend is written in (TS, Java, C#, or Go).

Not a bug — a deliberate design choice: the span answers "did this operation succeed from an observability standpoint" while the HTTP status answers "what does the contract returned to the caller say."

A declined charge that the handler fully handled (caught, with a clear reason returned) is a valid 200 response for the caller, but operations still needs it filterable — so the span status is set to ERROR and recordException (type, message, stack as a span event) so the trace UI shows exactly which operation failed and why.
The two signals serve different consumers and evolve independently: alerting thresholds can change without breaking any caller, and the API contract can change without losing failure visibility.

The boundary: a failure that was NOT handled (an exception that escapes) or a genuinely down downstream dependency is the server's fault and must be a 5xx together with an error span — the decoupling only covers business outcomes the handler actually processed, and must never be used to mask a real server error behind an HTTP 200.
The span must be end()-ed on every path, including the error branch, or it is never exported at all.
